Description: The user first can visualise data to assess quality at a first-glance, then specify whether either switch status will be used to filter data (i.e., removing and interpolating data marked as such by either switch).

While visualising raw recordings, the user can specify whether and how data will be cropped. This involves absolute cropping (i.e., removing data outside defined bounds from any further analysis), and 24-hour cropping (i.e., an additional crop which truncates kept measurements to an exact number of 24-hour timeframes). Differentiating cropping methods allows for more accurate rate calculations (i.e., keeping values both before and after 24-hour cutoffs). The user can also specify whether light status should define cropping (e.g., starting a 24-hour crop when lights turn 'on').

The user must input several mass filtering parameters to identify 'spikes (i.e., animal-device interactions), perform linear interpolation, and apply data smoothing. Different values can be iteratively tested to visualise  effects until the user specifies being satisfied with mass filters.

For messy datasets, this allows users to both identify which plateau, shift, and chip filters should be applied. Plateau filters ensure that data following prior measurements does not indicate mass decline (i.e., interpreted as mice eating less food or food being added to the holder), while shift filters determine the timeframe over which the plateau filter is assessed. The chip filter allows users to manually identify whether acute mass additions/removals occurred (e.g., a 'chip' of sawdust being placed atop the food holder and later removed) which are identified by spikes and declines in resulting mass measurements. Applying the filter shifts subsequent data points to the value preceding the flanked 'chip'. Appropriate 'chip filter' application can be confirmed if a change in any of the filtered plots (columns 2-4) is accompanied by no change in the unfiltered plot (column 1) as seen in the provided figure reference. As this is a manual and subjective adjustment, which can skew results if used incorrectly, all chip filters are automatically recorded in output metadata (ED - 10). Unless obvious artifacts are present, neither the chip nor plateau filter should be applied.

Processed mass data and raw interaction counts are derived according to iteratively-determined user-specified parameters. This yields the time rate of change for both food-intake and animal-device interactions.
Raw light recordings are processed to either retain raw/smoothed light readings, or to binarise light as being 'on' or 'off'.
All outputs are provided for the user to visualise and then confirm whether satisfactory. If not, the user can repeat all prior processing steps for the current dataset.
Provides an additional step in the case of small datasets, allowing the user to normalise/flip recordings to begin at light- or dark-onset.

The user may additionally compress data outputs to provide averaged/binned reports. This is ideal if subsequently exporting to graphing/statistical software which cannot handle long datasets, or if aligning with parallel measurements (e.g., DVC data binned per minute).
